Hon. J. II. KING (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved the third reading of Bill No. 234 to amend the Pension Act.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to move the following amendment, seconded by Mr. Guthrie:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"the bill be recommended to the committee of the whole house, with instructions that they have power to add thereto the following section as section 4:
4.	It is hereby declared that the Pension Act shall be construed and administered as remedial legislation, and that if there be a reasonable doubt as to the right of an applicant to pension the applicant shall be given the benefit of such doubt.
(2)	If the decision of the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada be reversed by the Federal Appeal Board acting within its statutory jurisdiction, the judgment of the Federal Appeal Board shall thereupon for all the purposes of the Pension Act be deemed to be and be the decision of the commission.
(3)	For the purposes of the Pension Act the disability on discharge of an applicant for a pension who actually served in the theatre of war shall in the absence of misrepresentation or concealment on enlistment be conclusively presumed to be attributable to military service."
I do not propose Mr. Speaker, to take any considerable time in speaking to this amendment. The matter has been discussed in committee and it is only necessary that I should make two or three observations to direct the attention of the House to the purpose intended. It will be observed that subseotion 1 of the proposed section declares that the act shall be considered and administered as remedial legislation. It is true that section 15 of the Interpretation Act

applying to all statutes passed by this parliament provides in terms that every statute:
-shall be deemed remedial, whether its immediate purport is to direct the doing of anything^ which parliament deems to be for the public good, or to prevent or punish the doing of anything which it deems contrary to the public good.
. But it will be observed there is no provision that such statute shall be administered as remedial legislation, and in this instance I submit it is desirable, having regard to the dbservations made by the Minister of Defence the other evening as well as by the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, that the Pension Act should be not only construed as remedial legislation but' administered as such, and if there is a reasonable doubt as to the right of an applicant for a pension that doubt should be resolved in his favour. By "reasonable doubt" is meant an uncertainty of mind, not based upon affection or prejudice, but representing a real and reasoned indecision from given facts. If there be a doubt or uncertainty under those circumstances, it may be designated as reasonable, and in the administration of the act that doubt should be resolved in favour of the applicant.
With respect to the second subsection of the proposed section, it is merely a provision to overcome the difficulty to which I directed attention the other evening. Where t'he pension board has been overruled by the Federal Appeal Board, that judgment, instead of remaining nugatory and inoperative, shall be deemed to be the decision of the commission itself, the word " commission " being defined by the statute to mean the Board of Pension Commissioners for Canada.
With respect' to the third subsection, there is of course much difficulty. It is true that post war condition has sometimes been directly referred back to the pre-war condition of a soldier who enlisted for service, and all that is hoped to be accomplished at this time -having regard to the statements made by the ministers the other evening that they are inquiring into the whole operation of the act-is to provide that where a soldier has been in the actual theatre of war his condition on discharge must be conclusively presumed to be the result of his service. In other words, it is not open for this Dominion to say that the condition of a soldier on discharge is attributable to his enlistment condition. If he was sound enough or of sufficiently good health to be attested and enlisted, it must be taken that if he served in the actual theatre of war there as conclusive presumption that such disability was caused by his military service.

Pension Act-Mr. Bennett
In regard to this, I hold in my hand a letter that I have received from a city in Ontario since I last addressed the House. The writer, a young man, says:
I saw a service in France, and when I state "service" I mean front line service from October 3 1916 to August 25, 1918, which includes the Somme, Vimy Ridge, Hill 70, Passchendale ridge. Amiens, Mount Kemmel and the commencement of the drive for Boulon Woods. In the latter all my company with exception of about eight men were badly gassed, myself being one that was gassed and invalided to England where I remained in hospital until about two weeks before armistice was signed. Now Mr. Bennett I think you will agree with me that whatever my disabilities were when 1 enlisted they surely were not improved any after two years of continuous privations. I think if my war service is checked up I missed seven or nine days of front line duty while out in France. I doubt whether there are many first division men with as much continuous front line duty to their credit, if credit be such.
Now, that young man when dealing with the question of a pension was confronted by the fact that prior to enlistment his health had not been as sound in one particular as he might have desired, and it was by the Board of Pension Commissioners concluded that a part of his disability was attributable to his prewar conditions. It is to overcome such a difficulty that this amendment has been suggested.
I have also a communication received from another town in Ontario, in which the young man says that he had a piece of metal in his eye, the wound entirely healed, and he thought his eye was all right, but he told the attesting officer that fact. He joined the flying corps and:
-while flying another plane flew across the tail of my plane at about four thousand feet which made me crash. Somehow I managed to pull up near the ground, how I don't know, but I landed upside down, bruised my head, hurt my ribs and lost the sight of my right eye and damaged my knee.
The pension authorities assumed that his disability should be 16 per cent instead of 20 per cent because he had the injury to his eye in the days of his youth, which he had entirely forgotten except to mention it when he was attested.	.
I bring these matters to the attention of the House in no party sense. I realize the difficulty of the minister with whom I have discussed the matter, and I realize also the difficulty there is in endeavouring to deal with the multitudinous cases that have arisen under the statute. My effort has been to deal with what I conceive to be those pressing cases Which should be dealt with so as to restore in some degree a sense of confidence
in the good faith of the country as a whole when we made the promise during the war that those who were disabled in the service of their country would be taken care of through our Pension Act. I am not unmindful of the many difficulties that have to be encountered in the administration of the statute, and I realize there are many, many suggestions that might be embodied in the form of amendments to this measure. The minister pointed out the other night that he proposed to reconsider and consolidate the Pension Act. I apprehend that the act will be consolidated by the commission dealing with the revision of the statutes. But he will revise and consolidate it during the recess and submit it to pailiament for consideration in the early days of next session. But I cannot think it desirable-nay, I do not think it is at all in the interests of the country as a whole-that at this time we should leave our places in parliament without at least making a declaration in the form of the amendments I have suggested. We ought in the first place to declare that it is our wish, wherever there be a reasonable doubt-and the word "reasonable" is always construed in the sense I have indicated-that such doubt be resolved in favour of the applicant, and that where any man has been attested as sound, after having seen service in the front line trenches in any theatre of war, to use the words of the statute, this country should be precluded and estopped from setting up that the condition of the soldier on discharge was not attributable to military service. I cannot, in any amendment I might suggest, deal with all cases that are likely to arise, but that is the general principle I lay down. The other difficulty concerns the relative position of the Board of Pension Commissioners and the Federal Appeal Board, and it is a difficulty that might readily lead, one might almost say, to public scandal. I suggest that wherever it is within the statutory jurisdiction of the Federal Appeal Board to hear an appeal, and wherever such an appeal has been heard and the judgment of the pensions board has been reversed, the judgment of the appeal board should become thereupon the judgment or decision of the Board of Pension Commissioners itself.
Respecting the general power of a private individual even to suggest amendments of this character, I realize the limitations that are imposed upon us. I therefore have endeavoured to eliminate any possible charge of having proposed new legislation involving the expenditure of public moneys. Rather, I have contented myself with making pro-
Pension Act-Mr. COMMONS
King (Kootenay)
oedural declarations calculated, in my judgment-it is of course entirely for the House to say to what extent these declarations re-flecl the general feeling-to make somewhat easier the way of those who have claims upon the state by reason of services they have given. Above all, I submit that what I propose will make for a more contented state of mind among the soldiers, a calmer and fairer appreciation, perhaps, of the difficulties under which the ministers are carrying on their duties. And these difficulties are quite serious in every country where pensions have to be awarded. I do commend these amendments to the House, and I do so in none but the most earnest desire, by means of these short provisions, to afford some temporary relief until such time as the government may be able to deal with the matter in more comprehensive terms.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. H. KING (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
On April 1 in
reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans), I intimated that the government, after having reviewed the mass of material submitted by various soldiers organizations in February of this year requesting amendments to the Pension Act and changes in the administrative regulations, had decided that the whole subject was so comprehensive that they did not feel they would be justified in altering this session the principle on which pensions had been heretofore granted. Our Pension Act, I pointed out, had been built up during the war. The present act passed in 1919, and the subsequent amendments thereto, have 'been the controlling instruments for the administration of pensions in Canada. It is well known to hon. gentlemen that the pensions board is composed of three members, a chairman and two others. The chairman has been associated with the administration of pensions since 1917. He ig a man of high educational attainments, with a good overseas record, and, I understand, is an eminent lawyer. He is the son of a former Minister of Justice and Prime Minister of this country.
A suggestion was made in the debate on April 7 that there had been a hardening in the administration. Well, that is difficult to say. We know that our pensions bill is growing from year to year. It may be that the act should be broadened, and I am satisfied that the people of Canada have every wish to deal justly with soldiers. I believe an attempt has been made by parliament to formulate legislation broad enough to realize that wish of the Canadian people. It is the duty of the government to interpret the will

of the people, and parliament is the plhce wherein the government may learn the point of view held by various sections of the country.
The act was brought into being in 1919 and was amended in the years 1921, 1922, 1923, 1924 and 1925. Probably the most important contribution to the amendment of our pensions legislation was due to the efforts of the Ralston commission, which was appointed in 1922. That commission has perhaps contributed more information and general knowledge to the consideration of one of the most important questions, if not indeed the most important, before the Canadian people than any other governmental activity, and out of it many far-reaching amendments were made to the statute in 1924 and 1925. My colleague, the Minister of National Defence (Mr Ralston), was chairman of that commission. He is now a member of the government, and with his wide -knowledge of all matters affecting the returned soldiers-a knowledge gained in the course of an extensive investigation into the subject-he will be invaluable to the government and to the people of Canada in dealing with our soldier problem. I indicated on April 7 that the government were of the opinion that this material submitted to us in February of this year should be thoroughly digested departmentailly and in government circles, and that such legislation as the government deemed necessary, in the light of the representations then made, should be prepared in the form of amendments and submitted to parliament at an early date at the next session.
It has been the practice of parliament and of different governments when important amendments were mooted in this connection to have the question under advisement submitted to a representative committee of the House. And is not that the wisest course?
I think it will be generally conceded that that has been the proper procedure; it has done more than anything else to keep our pensions administration out of party politics. I appeal to the House on this occasion to see to it that the same course shall be pursued in the future, and I will undertake as minister to see that all representations submitted in behalf of the soldiers shall be given serious consideration during the summer with a view tc having any amendments growing out of them referred to a special committee of the House at the next session.
Let me briefly refer to the amendments proposed this afternoon. I will not discuss them at any length; as, I think, it would be better for the Solicitor General (Mr. Cannon), with

Pension Act-Mr. Arthurs
his wide knowledge of the statute, to deal with these amendments. I wish however to direct the attention of the House to the third amendment. If the principle therein propounded should be adopted by this House we surely have introduced something new in connection with the granting of pensions in Canada, and I am told by the officers administering the act that it would entail a very large addition to our pensions bill. I am satisfied that on . the third reading of a bill this parliament will not wish to adopt a new principle of this character; if that principle is right, involving as it does millions of dollars, then it should be carefully considered and its effect made known not only to members of the committee but to members of this House. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the course originally suggested by myself, speaking for the government, should be followed at this time, and that the bill should not be referred back to the committee but should receive third reading.
Before the minister concludes would he say what principles contained in the amendment are new?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will understand that it opens the door very wide and brings in a new principle.

I have repeatedly
heard representatives of the pension board tell committees of this House that they deal with cases of a reasonable doubt, but of course we know they do not. What other is a new principle?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am told that it
opens the door very wide and will make a great difference in administration and in the cost.
Surely the minister does not raise the question of cost.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am not raising
any objection as to the cost, but I say parliament should be advised of that cost.

I must remind hon.
gentlemen that we are not in committee of the whole but are considering the third reading of this bill.

I did not quite catch the substance of the amendment of the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett). I would like to draw the attention of the minister to a case in my own city of Calgary, that of a man who had been afflicted with a form of Bright's disease before he enlisted. He said, "I was good enough to be taken into the force and I was anxious to serve, but I had this little
trouble." During the course of the war this disease was aggravated and he is now unable to do any work; he applied for a pension and was refused on the ground that his disability did not result from the war. I would like to know if this new pension act would apply' to cases of that kind, because the application of this man has been refused several times already.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I am trying to
indicate to the House that amendments of that character, which would enlarge the field of pensions, should be considered by a committee of this House rather than rushed through hurriedly, and that is why I am asking the House not to consider favourably the amendment that has been proposed. I am not taking exception to the amendment, but rather to the time of its presentation.

Would the act cover a
case such as I have referred to?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I could not say,
because each of these cases must be judged on its merits.

I am
fully in accord with the principle of the amendment. I will not take the time of the House to narrate instances of which I know, but as I have said before it does seem to me that the act is too rigid and does not permit of a sympathetic interpretation, which the amendment would seem to cover.

Just before the amendment carries, I would like to say a few words on this question. I have asked the minister on one or two occasions for certain information with regard to the number of appeals made to the appeal board, and the number which were successful. I have not those figures under my hand at present, but doubtless the minister has put them on Hansard. I would point out that whereas the committee which sat two years ago intended that all appeals should come before the appeal board, at present only those appeals are heard which have to do with the eligibility of a man for pension, and the board has nothing to do with the cessation of pension, with the increase or decrease of the amount, or with the diagnosis. That board simply says whether a man is or is not eligible for a pension, which does not cover the real cause of complaint. I am satisfied that the minister has not taken the best course in not having this question looked into during the present session; I believe it should have been done, and I sincerely hope that if the government press this to its absolute conclusion
Pension Act-Mr. Ward

to-day, they will make up their minds to have a committee appointed in the regular way next year in order to go into this matter regardless of what any other chamber or parliament in this country may or may not do.

I would not have risen at all in connection with this matter, except that I wish to state my hearty agreement with the amendment offered by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett). The minister in charge of this bill made some reference to the cost of these pensions, and pointed out that the amendment would broaden -the act. I do not see it in that light at all. It is not a question of broadening the act, but a question of giving equality of opportunity. I could enumerate a great number of cases which I have on file and which involve -the question of equality; I have one case in mind, that of a boy who enlisted in 1915, and who, when he left the army, was shown by his medical sheet to be blind in the right eye. I have repeatedly taken up the matter with the Board of Pension Commissioners and they insist that the boy was blind in that eye when he enlisted. If that was the case, and a partially blind boy was accepted by the examining officer, surely there must have been something seriously wrong. I knew this boy before he enlisted, and personally I am convinced that he was not blind at all. I merely mention that case because he is a chap who should be getting at least a 40 per cent pension, and has received nothing at all.
I remember the case of another boy, who was suffering from diabetes. He was accepted for service, spent three years in the army and came out a physical wreck. Since that time he has never been able to earn a livelihood, yet because his medical adviser told him he had suffered from diabetes before entering the army, he is debarred by the present law from participating in any pension. I think the government could do many worse things than accept the amendments of the hon. member for West Calgary; in fact I believe they are about five years overdue. I am sure any member of this House who has had occasion to visit the pension board and the appeal board during the last four or five years must be impressed with the difficulty experienced in getting consideration for returned men. That fact has resulted in our having demands from all over this country for the abolition of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, the pension board and the appeal board. I have had applications from returned men demanding that these organizations be abolished. Why? Because the returned men

believe that these organizations are not giving the service they should, and that they are costing too much for the service given. Personally I think that the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment should be abolished; I think it has outlived its usefulness. There ought to be ways and means of dealing with disabled returned men much more expeditiously and effectively, and at a lesser cost, than is the case at the present time. I was hoping that the government would accept the very moderate amendments of the hon. member for West Calgairy; it would relieve the members of this House of a great deal of difficulty. I can visualize in the next few years a continuation and an increase of the difficulties we are having in trying to get redress for returned men who are to-day suffering from grave disabilities incurred during their war service, but who cannot get justice done them under the present act.

I think this amendment is in the right direction and something that we have needed, for the last two or three years at any rate. I have had several cases brought to my attention of men who I think need a little more reasonable treatment by the pension board, and I would suggest to the minister that he should accept this very moderate amendment. I think that the men should not be asked to wait for another year till the government considers the proposal which seems to me to be so necessary and which, after all, is so very moderate in its character. The country can very well afford to pay whatever increase in expenditure would be neeessaiy if this amendment goes through. I hope the minister will change his mind and permit the amendment to pass.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext: I should like to express the same hope from another section of this corner. It does seem that there ought to be a -more generous interpretation of the act, and until the act can be changed the amendment would appear to be one way of overcoming the difficulty. I trust that we shall not be asked to wait for another year before doing something for the men who need help.

As the mover of the amendment has
stated, this is in no way a political matter, and should not be treated as such by -the House. Every member, no matter on which side he sits, is of one mind on the question at issue, and that is to treat the returned man in the best possible way. I have listened to speeches which have been made in the course of this

Pension Act-Mr. Cannon
debate by members who are more conversant, it may be, with the condition of the returned man than I am, perhaps myself. My contribution to this debate will have no reference to the technical side of the subject; I wish to state in a very brief way what the real meaning of the amendment suggested by the hon. member for West Calgary is, in so far as the law is concerned.
The hon. member suggests that the bill should be referred back to committee and that then we should insert in it three amendments. The first amendment may be summed up as meaning, that whenever a reasonable doubt exists it should be resolved in favour of the applicant, that is in favour of the soldier who is before the board seeking a pension. Everyone will admit that whenever a reasonable doubt exists the soldier should be given the benefit of it, so that the only question is whether the amendment proposed by my hon. friend is necessary or not. If I vote against the amendment proposed by the hon. member for West Calgary I do not wish my vote to be construed as meaning that I am against the principle of the amendment, but if I find that that amendment is useless under the existing law I think we should not insert it in the bill. What is the law as it actually exists? It is that the commissioners who are called upon to decide a case shall weigh the evidence to the best of their ability; and I need not recall to the House that the members of the board as at present constituted are competent in such matters. When a doubt exists there is absolutely nothing in the law as it is to-day which prevents that doubt from being resolved in favour of the applicant. The commissioners can take that course now.
But they do not.

And moreover not only is
there nothing in the law which prevents the applicant from being given the benefit of that doubt, but there are the provisions of section 15 of the Interpretation Act, which deals with all legislation that we have on our statute books, and which applies consequently to the Pension Act. My hon. friend from West Calgary says that clause 15 only mentions "interpretation" but that clause mentions "interpretation" when the law is to be applied.
It does not deal with administration.

If my hon. friend will
allow me, section 15 says that every act, and every provision and enactment thereof, shall be deemed remedial. There is no practical
object in inserting in an act what is actually -the law at the present time. My hon. friend in his amendment says:
It is hereby declared that the Pension Act shall be construed and administered-
"And administered."

-
-as remedial legislation.
"And administered." That is not in section 15.

If my hon. friend will
allow me, I am making my argument. It says:
It is hereby declared that the Pension Act shall be construed and administered as remedial legislation.
Now our law in our statute says:
Every act and every provision and enactment thereof, shall be deemed remedial, whether its immediate purport is to direct the doing of any thing which parliament deems to be for the public good, or to prevent or punish the doing of any thing which it deems contrary to the public good.
Therefore, the general rule is laid down that every piece of legislation is remedial. Let us now read the last part' of section 15, and here we come to what divides my hon. friend and myself:
-and shall accordingly-
These are instructions contained in our law:
*-and shall accordingly receive such fair, large and liberal construction and interpretation as will best ensure the attainment of the object of the act.
How can you attain the object of an act when you do not administer it? Therefore, I say that this section 15 applies to administration or it has no sense at all, and then I conclude that the first part of my hon. friend's amendment is useless because it is in the law already.
Coming to the second part, when he says that the benefit of a reasonable doubt must be given to the soldier, he is simply stating what the commissioners can do already. The only objection that can meet this point in my argument is the objection that has been raised by my hon. friend opposite when they say: But' they do not do it. My answer to that is very simple. If a judge does not interpret the law as it should be interpreted, and t'he way to interpret and administer the law is laid down in section 15 which I have just read, the remedy is not to amend the law in order to supply the defects in the mind of the judge, but to improve the judge and see that he interprets the law as it should be interpreted or else remove him. That is the sensible way of looking at things.
Pension Act-Mr. Cannon
Would the minister advocate removing the board?

I do not advocate that.
I am simply answering the argument. I am saying that gentlemen on the other side wish to put in our law an amendment which has absolutely no practical meaning, which does not add in any way to the existing law, and the reason which they give is that the commissioners in certain cases have not given t'he decisions they should have given. My answer is this: Suppose a judge is on the bench dealing with a criminal case, and for some reason or other his decisions are not in conformity with the law; are we to amend our criminal code in order to correct the misjudgment of the judge, or are we to see to if that the judge himself improves his decisions, either by removing him or by giving him directions that will guide him in his future decisions? I have no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the debate which has taken place will show to the board the mind of the representatives sitting in parliament, and that the commissioners, being apprised of what the members wish, will certainly follow the instructions of parliament; and as I say, they have in the law as it exists to-day everything needed to meet the objections which have been pointed out in debate in this House.
Coming to the second amendment, it deals with the case where there is a conflict between the pension board and the appeal board. This conflict arises-I ask my hon. friend from West Calgary to follow me in this and correct me if I am not right-simply over one point, naimely, when the pension board deems that the appeal board has rendered a judgment in matters which are outside their jurisdiction. That is the only point over which conflict arises between the two bodies to-day. It is a conflict as to their respective jurisdictions. Would we be removing that conflict by adopting this amendment, if it is adopted? Not at all. I call the attention of hon. members to the wording of this amendment:
If a decision of the Board of Pension Commissioners of Canada is reversed by the federal appeal	board acting within its
statutory jurisdiction-
So this amendment simply says this: When the federal appeal board gives a decision, if that decision has been given by the board acting within its statutory jurisdiction, then the judgment of the federal appeal board is final. But nothing is added by this amendment; the law says that already. Whenever the federal appeal board gives a decision within its jurisdiction, the law now says that

that decision is final; and whenever it gives a decision outside its jurisdiction, why should that decision be acted upon?
Is it not a fact that there are cases where the federal appeal board gives decisions favourable to the applicant for a pension, and yet he gets none.
Certainly, and I say that that is a state of affairs which ought to be remedied, but I add that the amendment introduced by my hon. friend would not remedy it.
Sure it would.

Perhaps my hon. friend will follow my argument before jumping at conclusions; that is all I ask him to do. The conflict between the two boards i3 a conflict which arises out of the fact that the jurisdiction of the appeal board is contested by the pension board. Now this amendment says that only decisions given by the federal appeal board which are within their jurisdiction shall be final. But the law says that already; this amendment does not improve things in any way; things remain exactly the way they are. The proper remedy would be to define that jurisdiction. The proper remedy would be, if we wish to extend the powers of the federal appeal board, to extend them, but the moment those powers are extended we should define their jurisdiction in such a way that there can be no possible ambiguity as to the extent of the board's jurisdiction. My hon. friend does not do that by his amendment. The first amendment has no meaning in law; the second amendment has no object in law; but this amendment, if I may say so, has another object, and the members of this House, if they do not examine carefully these amendments, will be placed under the impression, like some hon. members who have already spoken, that in voting against them they are voting against the soldiers and putting them in a more unfavourable position than they are in to-day. If these amendments improved the condition of the soldiers in any way I would support them, but I say it is useless to adopt these amendments because we would only be putting in the bill something that does not mean anything.
Coming to the third amendment, it seeks to change altogether the basis upon which pensions are to be granted. We may do that; we have the authority to do it, but should we not pause before doing it and ask ourselves this question. This bill is now up for its third reading. We are at a stage of our

Pension Act-Mr. Cannon
proceedings where there is very little opportunity to study the real consequences and meaning of this amendment. Is this the time to introduce in our legislation such a radical change? Why not follow the suggestion of the hon. minister, which is very fair? The hon. minister does not bar the door to any amendments. He does not refuse to the soldiers any improvement in the situation. He does not bind the government or this House to refuse any amendment in the future. On the contrary, he admits the situation offers features of such a nature that parliament should intervene and change the law. But he says, we must have time to consider these amendments. He says, "Let us see to it that the amendments which are adopted will be the result of mature consideration and not of hasty drafting of sections the significance of which is uncertain and indefinite. This is the stand we take. Is that not fair and reasonable?
Would the minister suggest that we stay here until the question of pensions to the soldiers has been properly arranged?

My answer is very simple. I have no objection to staying, and those who wish at this time really to improve the legislation which exists should not adopt the means of moving amendments to the third reading; the amendments should be submitted to a committee which would have time to consider them maturely.

Were those amendments
not submitted to the committee?
No.
Not discussed?

No, these amendments are the result of a general discussion which took place in this House, but they are drafted in such a way that two of them mean nothing, and the last one introduces in our system a new basis. Are we willing to accept that basis?
What is that?

The new basis, as far as the medical evidence is concerned, if I understand it, means that if a man has given his service at the front, the fact that he has enlisted and given that service will be sufficient to prove that any disability is attributable to his war condition.
This is on discharge.
Yes.
Has the government any alternative to meet the situation for this year?

Yes. First, when it comes to improving the law and amending it, we wish to have a committee composed of the most competent members on both sides of the House to examine the question, go into it to the fullest extent, and then bring to the House, to those who are less conversant with the matter, reports which will enable us to have the law as perfect as the human mind can make it. This is one suggestion made by the minister. Our second suggestion is that if there are really needy cases there is a clause already in our law, the meritorious clause, which enables the board to deal with them immediately. This is not a political matter in any way. All members of the House are of one mind. The principles that have been expounded by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett) and others in the House are principles in which we all join. Our only differences in views are as to the means and methods to be adopted to attain the object. These proposed amendments would not meet this object. They have been drawn up in such a way that they certainly do not mean what the hon. member for West Calgary intended them to mean.

I will take a chance on
that.

This is not a matter in
which we should take chances.

I will take a chance
that they mean what I intended them to mean.

We are dealing now with
the serious question of pensions. Are the members willing to take a chance on an amendment? Will they vote on an amendment, the meaning of which they are not sure of?

Then what chance have
the men who are in need of and entitled to pension of obtaining that pension before parliament meets again?

There is a meritorious
clause in the act.

How many cases
have been dealt with under that meritorious clause?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I understand
thirteen cases have been taken up, and others are under consideration. It is only recently that it has been made effectual.

Pension Act-Mr. Cannon
Does that fact not show that it has not been effective?
How long has that clause been in the act?

That would not matter.
I suppose the soldiers understand that if they apply to the board and their application is refused, it is final.
Mr, WOODSWORTH:	Would the hon.
member deny that the adjustment bureau has again and again tried to take advantage of that clause and finds it impossible to do so?

We are coming to the
same point. We admit we have in our law all the remedies which we need. For instance, if there is a needy case we have the meritorious clause. But the objections are that the board does not apply the law as it should be applied.
Change the law.

Again I come to the first
question I put to the House. If the law is badly interpreted by any tribunal in the land, are we to amend the law to meet the interpretation, or are we to improve the tribunal? We are going to have a vote on this question, and if the vote has any meaning, after examining these amendments as I have examined them, it is simply this: even if the two first amendments were adopted the condition of the soldier would not be improved. Are we going to make this a party question and divide the House when we have no practical object in doing so? Or are we going to say: "Here is a question that has to be settled. People are not satisfied, as they should be." Let us assume that during the recess this question is taken up by people -who are qualified to deal with it and competent to solve it, and at the opening of the next session a committee composed of the most competent members on all sides of the House will sit, examine the question and make a report. We will then be in a position to amend our law in order to meet the just demands made upon us, whereas if we try to introduce these amendments now we are simply confusing the issue.

I may say, Mr. Speaker,
that I waited on the board this morning and was informed that the minister acts under the meritorious clause.

The minister deprecated
dividing the House on party lines. Why is it necessary to do so? Why not let every member vote according to his judgment?
I was paired with the hon. member for St. John-Albert (Mr. MaeLaren). Had I voted I would have voted against the amendment.

I was paired with the hon.
member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Rheaume). Had I voted I would have voted for the amendment.
I was paired with the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard). Had I voted I would have voted for the amendment.
I was paired with the junior member for Halifax (Mr. Quinn). Had I voted I should have voted against the amendment.
I was paired with the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Wilson). Had I voted I would have voted against the amendment.
I was paired with the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw). Had I voted I would have voted for the amendment.

I was paired with the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). Had I voted I would have voted for the amendment.
Motion agreed to and bill read the third time and passed.

I wish to ask another question, and the minister can get this information probably at his leisure. speechtext: I shall be very glad to look that up.

I was struck with the
statement made in committee the other day of the very rapid decrease in the number of Indians in British Columbia, and it led me to make certain investigations with respect to the conditions in my own province. I cannot think that the medical service given to the Indians is all that it should bet, and I strongly urge the desirability of having better medical service for the Indians in Alberta. They have very valuable property which they occupy, they have substantial funds, and I feel that it is not very creditable to us that they should
Supply-Indian Affairs

be disappearing as rapidly as they are. It is not, to say the least, creditable to ns that so many of them have passed away so quickly, and I refer particularly to the children and to the younger men and women. I think that a better nursing service could be established in some of the reserves in Alberta, and more frequent medical attention given. The Indian is not always amenable to our methods of medical care, but I should like to ask the minister if he would have the matter looked into, and see what can be done to improve conditions. On the Sarcee reserve there has been very considerable improvement. I will not go into the details to-night, but I cannot urge too strongly the desirability of more careful supervision and better attention being given to the Indians than they now receive.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:

I think the work being done amongst the children will have a very beneficial effect; but undoubtedly if we are going to stamp out the plague of tuberculosis, it will require a great deal more money than we are spending on that work at the present time. However, I hope to get the service strengthened, and see if it is not possible to stamp out, in very large degree, this plague amongst the Indians of Canada.

Why should not the Six

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
In a great
many instances where there are day schools, they are erected by the religious organizations who are carrying on the work, sometimes out of the funds of the band, frequently assisted by the department. In the case under discussion the schools 'were constructed from the band funds of the Six Nations, but the usual assistance is given to the teachers such as is given to any other Indian school in Canada. But the residential schools are all constructed and paid for by the government.

I think there is some discrimination being shown in this matter against the Six Nations Indians. The fund which is in the hands of the government in trust for the Six Nations Indians was derived from the sale of Indian lands belonging to the Six Nations Indians. I do not think it is fair to the Six Nations Indians that the whole cost of their edcuational facilities should be borne by the band, when other Indians throughout the Dominion receive grants for education.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There is
really no difference between the system in vogue on the Six Nations reserve and that prevailing on many other of the reserves throughout Canada. In addition to that, the institution in Brantford called the Mohawk institute is maintained altogether by the government for the benefit of the Indians.

But the Mohaw'k institute

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
No, and
many of these residential schools are not on the reserve they are serving. The children are brought from the reserve to the school.

As I understand it, the
department is taking care of the education of all Indians throughout the country except the Six Nations band. They happen to have been fortunate enough in the early days because of the part they took in the revolutionary war, to have had a certain section of
land in western Ontario set aside for their use. Certain portions of that land were afterwards surrendered to the government in consideration of a certain sum of money. That money has been held in trust by the government for the Six Nations, except to the extent that it has been encroached upon by expenses paid out of it, and I say the Indians of the Six Nations reserve are entitled to be educated at the cost of the general public of Canada just as much as the Indians in any other portion of the Dominion.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am informed that they have never made any demand other than for the grant that is paid them. This is one of the oldest reserves, and perhaps one of the most highly civilized, and certainly one of the best cultivated reserves in Canada, and they have been pretty well taking care of themselves not only in an educational way but in an agricultural way as well. I think it is well that they should be encouraged to do so. I hope the day will come when all the Indians will be in a position to take care of themselves. As the days go by, and the effects of education are felt among the Indians there is no reason in the world why they should not take their place along with the white man and bear the same burden.

If, as the minister says, no
complaint has been lodged hitherto, I am lodging a complaint now on behalf of the Six Nations. It is time that there was a complaint lodged. These funds have been set aside for the benefit of the Indians, and the money belongs to the Six Nations; it does not belong to this Dominion. The people on the reserve in the township of Tusearora are paying, as I understand from the minister, the whole cost of their local education, the Mohawk institute at Brantford being maintained by a New England society formed in the old country many years ago. The Mohawk institute is not on the reserve, and I do not know to what extent the government assists in that, nor am I concerned with that at present, but I do say that if the Indians in other parts of the Dominion are educated entirely at the expense of this country the Indians of the Six Nations should to some extent at least derive assistance from the government.

The idea is
simply to bring an astronomer from outside of Canada for a period of one year to work with the staffs at Ottawa and at Victoria alternately. He may be from Germany this year, from England the following year and from Australia the succeeding year, but surely hon. gentlemen opposite will not claim that Canada possesses all the knowledge of astronomy and that there is nothing to be learned from other institutions.

know.

These matters should be
dealt with by our universities if $2,500 is to be offered some person to qualify in astronomy, which requires a knowledge of higher mathematics and the careful study of many subjects. Why should we give $2,500 to a foreigner, using the word in the broad sense, to come here and stay at Ottawa or Victoria for a year as astronomer, when we all know that $2,500 will not get a man worthy of being called an astronomer? What kind of man are you going to get for that amount? You will get a $2,500 man. The thing is wrong in principle; why should the money of the taxpayers go to pay an astronomer at $2,500, which will not secure a high class astronomer, while we lose an opportunity to offer a fellowship to a Canadian in one of our universities to go abroad and get a first-class working knowledge which we have not the facilities to give him. Isn't that the way to do it? More than that, what effect will it have upon the boys going to the universities in order to train themselves in astronomy? Should not this money go to some young man who desires to become a first-class astronomer, to permit him to go abroad and study at Greenwich or another of the great observatories? I submit the item should not pass.

I think we are approaching this from the wrong end. Obviously if you bring a man here you are giving him $2,500 with which to educate himself, because it is impossible to get a man for that sum to give instruction in our institutions. He would benefit from it, I dare say, but on the other hand if you take one of our students and send him abroad, he would get the benefit of the knowledge of all the professors of that institution. I would like to impress upon the minister that we are starting at the wrong end, and I move that the item be struck out.

Rather than strike
it out, if the minister is going to do something I would leave it there and let him go to McGill University and say, "We will give you a fellowship for one of your graduates in astronomy, to permit him to go abroad for a year and study and then come back to give us the benefit of his knowledge." Then go to Toronto and let Queen's be last, if you like. Remember our own Canadian universities, and give our students a chance to go abroad and gain this knowledge not only at one university, but in Germany this year, possibly England next year, and the United States the year after. I am not saying this for political reasons, but I am afraid that every astronomical student and professor in
