The individual gets the lands free for living on them for six months in the course of three years, paying a fee of $10, and performing certain other obligations. He then gets the ownership title in fee simple to the surface rights. Up to 1887 the base mineral rights went with the crown lands. In that year the system was changed and the mineral rights were retained for the crown and sold and subsequently leased to anyone making application for them. I want to say that as regards doing injury to the surface every precaution is taken to protect the owner of the surface rights. He cannot, of course, prevent mining operations upon the land by the individual who takes the lease, but his interest is protected and, of course, he has the same right as any other individual to file on the mineral rights if he desires to do so. My hon. friend pointed out that he does not always know when applications are being made, or when a certain district is liable to produce minerals, he does not know perhaps until the rights are gone. But in our own province, with one or two exceptions,
I have not heard of any very serious hardship. I would be prepared to say at once that I would go the full length of protecting the owner of the surface rights, but as we only collect now the royalties between 2i and 5 per cent, there is not very much hope of giving anything to the owner of the surface rights in the way of royalties. In the period of seven or eight years in which I have been dealing with the leasing of lands, both surface and under-surface, particularly in the search for oil, there have been millions and millions of dollars expended, not uselessly but in development work to locate oil. The locating of oil is a pretty expensive proposition at best, and as my hon. friend knows there are only two localities in the province of Alberta that give promise of being oil fields at the present. One is very close to his own home in the Turner valley. An immense amount of money has been spent in attempts to obtain oil and gas in the province of Alberta. The securing of gas has been fairly successful, but it cannot be said that .the securing of oil, considering the amount of money that has been spent upon it, has been entirely successful. So far as I am concerned I am willing to enact regulations that will give full protection to the owner of the surface rights, and if he suffers injury as my hon. friend has pointed out on account of the odour arising from the natural gas, that flows from these wells, assuredly in the event of any injury being done to his land he should secure full
compensation for the same. If the regulations are not sufficiently wide to do that, I would be quite prepared to make them wide enough to cover any injury of that character.
Mr. CO'OTE: I am very glad that the minister is sympathetic enough to say -that he will change the regulations to protect these men. May I point out to him that all that is necessary to secure these men is simply to make a change in the regulations? If is possibly true that not a great many people are as yet affected by this matter which I have brought to the minister's attention, but I do think there is no doubt that in the years to come hundreds of thousands of acres of land are going to be filed on for oil leases, and this trouble is going to grow all the time. No doubt there will be in the future many cases of hardship just in line with the one I pointed out the other day. I do not think it will hinder the development of the oil fields of Alberta if a change were made requiring 5 per cent royalty to be paid to the owner of the surface rights. On the Stony Indian reserve, quite close to the Turner valley, the holder of an oil 'lease must pay 10 per cent royalty to the Indian department out of all the oil that he gets, as well as pay a dollar a year per acre rental. Now that is not stopping development on the Stony reserve because I am told there are several wells being drilled there. I cannot see how 5 per cent royalty for the owner of the surface rights would hold up development of lands outside of the reserve. Some of these oil wells are great wealth producers. The Royalite well is, I am informed, producing annually to the value of one and a quarter millions; it is one of the greatest wealth producing wells in the world. It is true that the others are not quite as large producers, but they are giving handsome returns to the companies that have drilled the wells. I do not want to delay the minister's estimates at all but I should like him to give very careful consideration to this matter. I am sure that the owners of the surface rights are entitled to more protection than they are getting to-day, and I think the most satisfactory manner of protecting them would be to give them a small royalty of five per cent. That is a very small royalty. Most of the men who secured these leases are speculators who came in between the government and the oil companies, and they are the ones who are getting a royalty in almost every case. I think it would be much better to have a small royalty go to the holder of the surface rights, and less go to the speculator who comes in between the government and the oil companies that do the drilling.
Supply-Interior

Who owns the oil under
the land in the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I am
speaking only of federal crown lands.

The question I was
coming to was this:	If the people in
Ontario who own the land and got it from the government also own the oil, why should not the same apply to the people in the northwest? Why should the government retain the oil for themselves out there? It seems to me an absurdity. The people who own the land are entitled to the oil. I am quite content to leave the metals to the crown, because they belong to the crown, but the oil should belong to the people who own the land.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
The
Hudson's Bay Company when they sold their rights to Canada reserved in the area which the company retained, the base metals, which, of course, include oil. The Canadian Pacific Railway got large tracts of land to assist in the building of their railway and they own the oil rights. Up until 1898 the homesteader who homesteaded these lands owned the base metals under his lands.
Until 18S7.

In Ontario the Canada
Land Company-

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: If my hon. friend will sit down and calm himself I will give him an answer.
If you will only come to an answer.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I will come to it at. once. I still think if we are to have oil development in the northwest and in the Northwest Territories some assistance will have to be given, and it has been given, to encourage development work for the purpose of discovering oil. I am free to say that very little has been done by the government in that respect, but if these oil rights were owned by the individuals owning the land I am bound to think that development would be retarded to a very great degree.
No.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
Then we
differ, but that is my opinion, and I have been dealing with this matter for five years.

The minister may have
full information on the subject, but how do they do in the United States? Is there any lack of development there? The people who

develop oil take leases from the owners of the land. We have the development of gas and oil in Ontario, and I can tell the minister that in Ontario the oil fields do not pay nearly as well as those in the northwest. The wells are much shallower in Ontario, and they are not as good producers. Out west when you get a well, you get something, but with us it is different. In Pennsylvania, right opposite from Ontario, the oil goes with the land. There is no doubt about that, and it should go with it.

I do not want to delay
the committee but I would point out that in the state of Montana right across the line from us there is far more oil development than there is in Alberta. There is a reason for that. Most of the -wells in Montana are much shallower than those in Alberta. I do not think it would have retarded development if the owners of the land had been given the oil along with the surface rights. I do not think that at this time we can give the oil to the owners of the land, because in so many cases where the oil has been withheld from the owner of the surface rights, it has been leased by the government to speculators or to the oil companies. Under the regulations now in force an oil company can hold thousands of acres under lease by just drilling one well, and the amount they spend in drilling can be credited up against the rent they owe the government on account of the lease.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: Only in the development stage, only until they strike oil.

I think if the owners had
been given the oil rights these oil companies would have gone in and made an agreement With a number of farmers or owners of land m a certain district until they had got all the oil leases they wanted. That is the way it is done in the United States, on a straight royalty Dasis, and as a rule the men in a certain neighbourhood are willing to sign up with the company on a royalty of probably ten per cent. The company then know just what they must pay to secure the oil, but under our system the government leaves it largely in the hands of the company to say what royalty they will pay, and they can change it from time to time. I would ask the minister how many acres a company may hold and how far apart the different leases may be that a company acquires and controls simply by the drilling of one well.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I have not the regulations with me, but the most they are credited with is only 50 per cent of the cost of the development work, to be applied

Supply-Interior
against the rental. There have been amalgamations of leases, but one individual is entitled to hold only 1,920 acres. I have forgotten the restricted area to which the leases are limited, but it is not a very large area.

To interest the rest of the
committee in this case, I might say that the Hudsons' Bay Company and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company were granted all the mineral rights in connection with their lands, except as regards gold and silver. I hope the committee will see what an unfair position the rest of us were placed in, because we were given only the surface rights, while these two great corporations get the surface rights and everything underneath as far down as they care to go. I do not think we have used our pioneers fairly, and all I am asking is, not that you give them the mineral rights underneath the land, but that you say when any company or owner or lessee of the mineral rights is going to go in and drill, the 'owner of the land shall be given a royalty of five per cent; that is only one-twentieth of the oil that might be found, and if no oil is found the holders of the lease will not be required to pay anything. If, on the other hand, they secure a good well, the owner of the surface rights gets a royalty of five per cent. It is true that most of these men when they got their patent did not know that the oil rights were being withheld from them, and some of them are anxious to fight the case in the courts, because they hold that oil is not a mineral. I am not a lawyer and would hesitate to express an opinion on that point, but the Department of the Interior could easily settle the dissatisfaction that exists out there by giving these men a royalty of say five per cent.

The hon. member from Macleod labours under a misapprehension with respect to part of the situation. When the lands in the west were homesteaded, the original patents issued by the crown conveyed to the patentee all the oil, all the gas, and all the minerals under the land except gold, silver and copper. The grants to the railways also conveyed to them all the minerals under the land except the precious metals. The land grant to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company carried with it oil and gas rights, and the rights to other minerals except th* precious metals. The grant to the Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company also carried with it all the minerals except the precious metals. It was thought by the government of the day between 1896 and 1911 that there
was good reason for contesting the right of the Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company to the mines and minerals under the land. Litigation followed. The case went to the Privy Council and it was decided that the railway company had the right to the mines and minerals; that included oil and the natural gas. When the Hudson's Bay Company, whose patents also gave them mines and minerals, except precious metals, sold lands; when the Canadian Pacific Railway sold lands; when the Calgary and Edmonton Railway Company sold lands, they reserved to themselves the mines and minerals, the coal, the oil, the natural gas, but not, however, the gold and silver, which still belong to the crown. In 1887 a regulation was passed following a statute by which thereafter the crown reserved in all patents the mines and minerals. The pioneers have patents that convey to them the oil and natural gas. Such patents the minister encounters every day. Hence it is that we find in one part of Alberta a man who owns a quarter-section owning the natural gas and the oil, because his right to the patent accrued before the change in the law. What happens now is that the whole of southern Alberta is blanketed by leases issued by the crown conveying to the lessee the right to the oil and natural gas, and in some instances the coal beneath the surface of lands which have been patented with these reservations. It seems strange, but the fact is that the railway companies are receiving substantial sums of money from royalties on oil and natural gas, and this country, within the next few years, if the oil development in Alberta is worth anything near as much as is probable, will be receiving not less than $1,000,000 for royalties. This parliament forgets that. The reservation made in favour of the crown in right of the Dominion, which will one day pass to the provinces when they obtain their natural resources, will bring in a million dollars a year if the development is anything like it is expected to be. The difficulties referred to by my hon. friend from Macleod are real ones. They arise out of the past legislation. The minister can do nothing now for t'he obvious reason that leases are outstanding blanketing the whole territory from almost the northern part of Alberta to the boundary line, and those leases carry with them a rental, but that rental may be absorbed to the extent of fifty per cent if the owner of the lease will go upon the land and drill for oil. The minister is not entirely responsible for that regulation. It was almost the last act done, I think, by the government of 1921.
Supply-Interior

Oil drilling operations were being carried on m Alberta, and a revolving credit was established in order that there might be some measure of development in that province, and the cost of the development to the extent of fifty per cent thereof was applied to payment of rentals to the crown. Those who did not develop lost their leases, and those who did develop paid rentals by work. Over four millions have been spent by one company in development in Alberta. That expenditure has produced nothing in the way of results, except at the Royalite well which has been profitable. That position is well known to all of us who reside in Alberta. The efforts the government made might have been made in another way by expending public money in development, but instead of spending public money they expressed a willingness that fifty per cent of the money expended by oil operations should go to pay rent, thereby ensuring that over given areas holes were to be sunk t'o ascertain whether a profitable oil field can be developed in that province. Up to the present there is no conclusive evidence that we have a commercial oil area in Alberta. In Montana south of Alberta they have t'he Sunburst field, but the structure apparently does not extend north of the forty-ninth parallel, and up to this moment' we have no substantial quantities of crude oil in that locality. We have crude naphtha, which has been extracted from natural gas, but we have not been able to secure any quantity of petroleum. We have one place in that' district where the well produces about fifty barrels of crude oil per day. It is not the class of crude oil they are seeking, but it is an indication that there may be an oil pool under the surface. One well is a mile deep. Another well went down five thousand feet, and t'hey have not secured results that warrant the assumption that they will be able to find oil at less than four thousand feet. The minister is powerless t'o break the outstanding leases. He could not pay a royalty to the farmer who owns the surface. When he bought his land his contract did not give to him subsurface rights to oil and gas. He has a right' under his contract with the railway or under his patent to demand a reasonable compensataion for the surface used and occupied in sinking an oil well, but the operator is not subject to the caprice of the owner in that regard. If the land owner and operator do not' agree upon the amount to be paid it is settled by arbitration. It is natural that when natural gas is found beneath a homestead the homesteader should expect to receive some benefit' from it, but when he looks at his patent he finds he is only entitled to the surface subject to the right of the 
crown, or company or lessee to the subsurface rights, and the government or company will receive the royalties if gas or oil is found there. The oil leases up to 1930 do not provide for the payment to the crown of a royalty. The right to seek for and to discover oil and market it without payment of royalty was supposed to be an incentive to carry on such operations. But after 1930 royalty is payable, which roy-alt.y, with respect to natural gas and naphtha in the case of one of the railways, already amounts to approximately $90,000 per annum. If operations are successful the money the province will obtain in the way of royalties, will compensate the province of Alberta when they secure their rights for the loss sustained by the pioneers and owners of the surface by reason of their not being the owners of the subsurface rights. But this advantage is more apparent than real until they succeed in discovering oil. Until that time there is no benefit. But when 1930 is reached, and the resources pass to the province of Alberta, that province in a very short time will be receiving as a minimum, outside of taxes-and the taxes are considerable-at least a million in a year as royalties, which will mount to five million a year or more if the developments materialize as we hope.
I do not know how the minister can deal with the situation. I have had occasion to look into the matter many times, I quite agree with my hon. friend from Macleod, but there is no method other than for the government to compensate those who have obtained leases in good faith for the losses they have sustained by reason of being placed in the position they occupy. But there is no reason to adopt that course, because the government is holding these resources as trustees, as one day they will pass to the western provinces. There will be no change in respect of that. It will be the crown in the right of the province rather than the crown in the right of the Dominion. We all hope that that day may be not long distant, even though it may result in depriving the Minister of the Interior of any work in his department.
The hon. member stated that there is only one oil field in southern Alberta. Surely he does not claim that there is no oil in the Wainwright field?

I am glad my friend from Battle River has made that observation. From the standpoint of commercial success there is not yet a producing oil field in Alberta, but there has been a very valuable natural gas field, the most valuable except one in the world, and crude naphtha has been successfully abstracted in very profitable quantities

Supply-Interior
from the original Royalite well in the Turner valley. According to reports that appear *in the newspapers from time to time the yield represents a value of about a million dollars a year. Outside of that, every person who has put any money in oil has experienced not dividends but losses. As to what my hon. friend from Lincoln says, the question is entirely different in Ontario from what it is in our territory. My friend from Macleod put the issue very clearly when he said that it is contended that perhaps oil is not a mineral. I will merely put it to my friend in the way it was put by a very eminent judge not long since. All substances taken from the soil must be animal, mineral or vegetable; oil is neither a vegetable nor an animal substance; therefore it must be a mineral. In those few short sentences that eminent judge in an older civilization than this dismissed the claim that oil is not a mineral. I cannot add anything to his observation.

I should like to make it clear that I am not objecting to the policy the department has adopted of allowing development work to apply on rentals due under a lease, but I would say that the holder of such lease so far as I can see has no right to the surface except under regulations which are made by the crown-the Department of the Interior in this case.

In the patent issued to the owner of the soil the reservation is made that it is subject to a grant being made by the crown to any lessee to enable him to mine minerals owned by the crown. That is the basis of the whole matter.

Admitting that that is so, I still hold that the terms upon which he can enter on the land must be determined by the regulations-made by the Minister of the Interior. All I am asking is that the minister should insert in the regulations a condition that the compensation to be given to the owner of the surface rights shall be a royalty of five per cent on any oil or gas taken from the property. It seems to me there is nothing impossible about it. It is the most feasible way of giving the owner of the surface rights some equitable protection.

There is no doubt that it might be done, but it could not be done with
respect to existing leases.
The longer the matter is neglected the more difficult it will be to deal with it.

In 1914 when we first had the oil craze in Alberta a number of companies were floated, but since then nothing has been heard of them. Since the new oil boom started a number of shareholders in those old companies have tried to get information from the department as to what happened to the leases they held, how they were transferred, and so on. On behalf of a large number of such shareholders I applied to the department for information regarding certain affidavits that had been made for transfers of leases, as we had good reason to believe that those affidavits were not true, but the department would not give us any information.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I do not understand why my hon. friend should not get full information. In all probability the leases were cancelled, but he should have been furnished with the fullest information.

Let me give the minister an instance. The regulations require that the head office of the company shall be in His Majesty's dominions; and at one time all the directors were required to be British subjects, but this requirement has since been changed. Now, somebody made an affidavit that the head office of a certain company was in His Majesty's dominions, when as a matter of fact it was not. We tried to find out who made the affidavit, but the department refused to give us any information.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I know of no reason for withholding such information. If my hon. friend still desires to get it I will see that it is furnished to him.

Mr. Chairman, Alberta is not the only place on the face of the earth where there are oil fields to-day. Probably the most active oil prospect in western Canada at the present time is in the district of Grand View in Manitoba. Last summer an American oil prospector located in that district, shipped in a drilling outfit, and is supposed to have discovered oil. The greater portion of the district was originally homestead lands. A short time ago a very small area there changed hands for $132,000. I think this shows that the suggestion of the member for Macleod should be given very serious consideration. Oil promoters from Winnipeg and other points come in and buy up leases at fifty cents an acre and sell them to an oil company at a greatly enhanced price, while the original owners of the land get no royalties whatever upon any oil that may be found under their property. They are not even given an opportunity of leasing the land that they have been farming for the last thirty years. Upon my word, I cannot un-



Supply-Interior
derstand the reasoning of the member for West Calgary. Why cannot this parliament enact a law requiring any oil promoter to pay to those owning the surface rights a royalty on any oil that may be produced? I am not a lawyer, but my common sense makes me believe that this parliament could pass a law to that effect. Morally I think it should be done. I hope the minister will give this matter his very serious consideration.

Two or three years ago I brought the question of the transfer of oil leases to the attention of the minister. In the city of Calgary to-day he will find oil leases being peddled on the street and advertised for sale. Is it the practice of the department to allow these speculative ventures to proceed when transfers are asked for? Perhaps the minister will explain how the transfers are made.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: It was about the year 1922 that certain changes were made in the regulations by which a lessee might transfer a divided portion of his location. Formerly there could be no transference except for the whole of the lease of 1920 acres, but in order to encourage the small investor to take advantage of his opportunity, and not to shut him out altogether and create a monopoly for the rich companies, we made the reduction. As hon. gentlemen will know, many of the small companies were made up of stockholders of quite limited means.
Many of them with five or ten dollars.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
I do not
know about that. At any rate we tried to enable the small investor to cooperate with others and so reap some advantage. Otherwise there would be no development except by the large companies who would entirely exclude the small men. There is of course the other evil of investors taking leases and waiting for other people to do the developing. Altogether it is a difficult matter to devise regulations that will cure all evils. The plea put up to me was that the regulations shut out the small men altogether. They were squeezed out and eventually lost their money, and it was to help them that we cut down the lease and allowed [DOT] its transference in the event of all rentals having been paid up beforehand. That explains why the leases were allowed to be subdivided. It is useless to begin sinking a well with less than $30,000 or $40,000.

What is the maximum
acreage which anyone is allowed to hold.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: I am not sure. A number of the companies sometimes get together and drill one well, then apply 50 per cent of the amount expended on the well in the payment of rentals for the whole of the property.
The government should not allow speculators to get control of a lease merely to wait until someone desires to obtain it and then proceed to develop the property.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext:
There are
development clauses in the regulations.

I do not know of anything that, discourages development more than the speculator who waits for somebody to come and purchase the lease. The department should be more active in looking after this phase of the business. In Calgary to-day you will find dozens of oil leases advertised in store windows and in the newspapers. These leases can be secured for a consideration. Speculation has been the curse of the west and the department is not doing anything to relieve the situation. Not very far from where I live a certain company a few years ago drilled two or three wells, and in order that they might get hold of a large block of leases they usually got returned men in Calgary or Edmonton, to whom they gave the necessary funds, to secure the leases which were afterwards transferred back to the company. They gave $10 for the time the returned men spent securing the leases. In the particular area I have in mind the company had carried on a certain amount of development work, but for some mysterious reason they ceased drilling and instead capped their wells.

speakerposition: Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior
speechtext: What company?

It was in the Monitor field. The committee would like to know what is in these wells. After a certain amount of development has taken place, and before the companies are allowed to cap the wells, the department should ascertain what is in them. Knowledge is what is needed in this matter and I suggest that some steps be taken to find out what the wells contain. I do not want to deprive any company of the fruits of its labour, but at the same time any knowledge derived as the result of the granting of a lease from the crown should be regarded as the property of the department.

We have
full authority in the case of crown lands to make an examination, and we have a staff in Calgary kept doing that work; but we are prohibited from entering private lands.
